title: A Morning Spot Check for Noticing Change
markdown:
# A Morning Spot Check for Noticing Change

Many readers want a regular reflection habit but struggle to find a starting point that does not feel like another task on a list. One way to begin is to tie the exercise to a physical place you already visit. The place becomes a steady reference point while the details around it continue to change. This approach draws on the theme of impermanence: nothing in the spot stays exactly the same from day to day, yet the spot itself remains available to you.

A fixed location also lowers the effort required to start. You do not need to find silence, set a timer for twenty minutes, or adopt a new posture. You only need to arrive where you already go and pay attention for a short time.

This practice is drawn from an English-language guided reflection ebook. Digital access is sold through the owned checkout page.

## Pick a Place You Return To

Choose a location you pass through or sit in at about the same time each day. It can be a kitchen chair, the edge of your bed, a bench near your workplace, or a bus stop. The spot does not need to be quiet, comfortable, or visually pleasing. What matters is that you can return to it without extra effort.

If you work from home, your desk corner might work. If you commute, the same train platform or coffee shop counter can serve. The goal is consistency of place, not comfort or aesthetics. Once you have chosen the spot, commit to using it for at least one week before deciding whether to keep it or switch.

## Name Three Things That Are Different

When you arrive at your spot, spend two minutes looking around. Identify three details that are different from the last time you were there. They can be small and sensory:

- The angle of light on the floor
- A cup left in a different position
- The sound of traffic outside
- The temperature on your skin
- A leaf that has moved on a nearby plant

Say the differences quietly to yourself or write them in a note. You do not need to explain why they changed. The exercise is only to see that they have. If you cannot find three differences, look for smaller ones. A smudge on a window, a shift in shadow, or the weight of your bag on the floor all count.

## Finish With One Thing That Remains

After noting three differences, find one detail that is the same as before. It might be the grain of the table, the color of the wall, or the shape of the chair. Acknowledge it without holding on to it.

This last step keeps the practice from turning into a hunt for problems. It simply recognizes that change and stability appear together. You are not trying to fix anything. You are only noticing what is present and what has shifted.

Common obstacles include forgetting to stop, judging whether a difference is important enough, or feeling that nothing has changed. If you forget, simply resume the next day without trying to make up for the missed session. If a difference seems minor, count it anyway. The practice is not about finding significant events. It is about training attention to notice small shifts.

An Example for Today

Imagine you sit at the kitchen table with your morning coffee. Today you notice:

1. The sunlight hits the table two inches farther to the left than yesterday.
2. The spoon rests beside the mug instead of behind it.
3. The window frame has a small smudge you did not see before.

Then you notice one thing that is the same: the wood grain under your coffee cup remains unchanged.

That is the full practice. It takes under three minutes and requires nothing but your attention. You can repeat this tomorrow at the same spot, or pick a new spot if your schedule changes. The repetition itself is the reflection. Over time, you may begin to notice change without needing to sit down first.
